0.title: The Gospel and the Slave: Paul's Letter to Philemon
0.overview:
Philemon is the most personal of Paul's surviving letters — a private request from a prisoner to a friend on behalf of a runaway slave. Twenty-five verses. No doctrinal argument, no community disputes, no eschatological vision. Just a man writing to a man about a third man, in the most careful and emotionally loaded prose Paul ever produced. That it was preserved in the canon at all — and that Marcion included it in his truncated collection — tells us that the early church recognized something here that went beyond private correspondence.

The situation is this: Onesimus, a slave belonging to the wealthy Colossian Christian Philemon, had run away. By Roman law, a runaway slave was a thief — he had stolen himself, depriving his master of the economic value of his labor, and possibly taken money or property in the process (v. 18 implies some kind of financial debt). He had somehow — the details are not given — come into contact with Paul, then imprisoned in Rome (or possibly Ephesus), and had been converted. He had become genuinely useful to Paul in his imprisonment. And Paul was sending him back, letter in hand.

The letter is a masterpiece of rhetorical strategy. Paul never commands Philemon to free Onesimus — he appeals, he hints, he presses, he places moral weight. He frames Onesimus as his own child (v. 10), his very heart (v. 12), a beloved brother (v. 16). He writes a personal financial guarantee for any debt (vv. 18–19). He expresses confidence that Philemon will do 'even more than I say' (v. 21). And he announces that he is coming to stay (v. 22). By the end of the letter, Philemon cannot refuse without refusing Paul himself — and refusing Paul means refusing the gospel they both serve.

Where was Paul imprisoned? Most likely in Rome, around AD 60–62, the same imprisonment from which he wrote Colossians, carried by Tychicus with Onesimus (Col 4:7–9). Some have suggested Ephesus, which was nearer to Colossae and would make a runaway’s journey and Paul’s hoped-for visit (v. 22) easier. But Rome is where Acts leaves Paul under guard with freedom to receive visitors (Acts 28:30), and a runaway slave could hope to disappear in the capital.

The deepest theological claim of the letter is in v. 16: Onesimus is to be received 'no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother … both in the flesh and in the Lord.' The gospel does not erase social realities; it transforms them. Onesimus is still a man with a history, a legal status, a relationship with Philemon that has been damaged. But he is now a brother — in the flesh (as a human being) and in the Lord (as a fellow Christian). These two dimensions must operate simultaneously. Paul is not calling for the abolition of slavery in this letter; he is doing something more radical in the long run — he is planting a theological seed that makes slavery incompatible with Christian brotherhood.

1.title: Grace and a Brother: The Complete Letter
1.overview:
Onesimus, a slave of Philemon at Colossae, had run away, probably with some of his master’s money. In Rome he met Paul in prison and became a Christian. Paul now sends him home with this letter, asking Philemon to receive him not as a slave but as a beloved brother, and to charge any debt to Paul’s account.

The letter is a model of persuasion that leaves the other person free. Paul sets aside his authority and asks Philemon to extend the grace already at work in him to the one person he had not counted. One word, splanchna (“heart”), runs through it (vv. 7, 12, 20). And the gospel itself is acted out: a debtor is received on the account of another, who pays what he owes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greeting already does the letter’s work: Paul writes as a prisoner, not an apostle, and to the whole church that meets in Philemon’s house.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Credential He Sets Down

Paul opens not with his office but with his chains, and addresses a letter about one man's slave to the whole church in that man's house.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church in the house would all hear the letter read together.

Now: Paul makes the decision public among believers and trusts what the gospel has already done in that house.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker and Apphia our sister and Archippus our fellow soldier, and the church in your house:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Philemon is Paul’s shortest letter and his most personal: a single page about a runaway slave. Onesimus had fled from his master Philemon, a Christian in Colossae, perhaps after stealing from him. He met Paul in prison and became a believer, and now Paul sends him back with this letter, asking Philemon to welcome him, not as a slave but as a beloved brother. The letter is the gospel in miniature: reconciliation, substitution, and a new family in Christ that transforms the deepest social divisions. Luther said we are all Onesimus, and anyone who reads this page with care will find himself in it: the runaway, the debtor, the one who is received on another man’s account.

The setting. Philemon was a well-to-do believer at Colossae whose home hosted a church. He had probably been converted through Paul, perhaps in Ephesus (v. 19; Acts 19:10). Onesimus was his slave. Under Roman law, a runaway slave could be severely punished: flogged, branded, even crucified. Paul was in prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62, when he wrote Colossians; Onesimus travelled with Tychicus, who carried it (Colossians 4:7–9). Some suggest Onesimus deliberately sought out his master’s friend to plead his case, a recognised practice.

A prisoner for Christ Jesus. Not an apostle. About to ask a slave owner to do something extraordinary, Paul begins by laying down the one credential that could have compelled it. Everything in this letter is calculated to leave Philemon free. And the Lord Jesus became a prisoner for us before Paul was ever a prisoner for him: he was bound in a garden, led from court to court, and laid aside all his rights, so that runaways could be brought home.

And Timothy our brother. A second name on a private letter about a domestic matter: Philemon is going to know that someone else has read this.

Our beloved fellow worker. Philemon had worked with Paul in the gospel, perhaps by hosting the church.

And Apphia our sister. Probably Philemon’s wife, who would have managed the slaves day to day. Paul names her as a sister, a member of the family that Onesimus has just joined.

And Archippus our fellow soldier. Perhaps Philemon’s son, and a minister in the church, the man told in Colossians 4:17 to fulfil the ministry he had received.

And the church in your house. The early churches met in homes (Romans 16:5). Paul has addressed a letter about one man’s slave to the entire congregation that meets in that man’s living room, who will watch what Philemon does next.

Christ is all, and in all. The church in Philemon’s house would hear another letter from Paul at about the same time, with a sentence that this little letter puts to the test: here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all (Colossians 3:11). What gathers in Philemon’s living room is not the master’s family with his slaves at the back, but people who all belong to the same Lord.

Isn’t addressing the whole church a kind of pressure? Yes, and Paul knows exactly what he is doing. But look at the kind of pressure. He does not command, threaten, or invoke his office. He simply makes the decision public, among brothers, and trusts what the gospel has already done in this house. There is a difference between manipulation, which hides its aims and works on fear, and honest appeal, which says openly what it wants and leaves the other person free. In a church, the way a believer treats someone who has wronged him is not only his own business; it shows the family what the gospel is.
verseByVerse.note: Philemon was a well-to-do believer at Colossae whose home hosted the church. Apphia may have been his wife and Archippus his son. Paul wrote from prison, sending this letter with Colossians.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace to you and peace. The letter is bracketed by grace (v. 25), and grace is precisely what Paul is asking Philemon to extend. The question the letter puts is whether a man who has been dealt with on those terms can bring himself to deal with someone else the same way. Peace is things put right, a pointed word to open a letter about a broken household.

From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. “You” is plural: Paul is still speaking to the room. One word will do quiet work all the way through: Lord. Kyrios is the ordinary Greek for master; it is the word a slave used of the man who owned him. Philemon is Onesimus’s kyrios. Paul opens by naming a Lord above them both, and by the end he will ask Philemon to receive his slave as a brother, because they now share one.

How do I show grace to someone who has wronged me, when I do not feel gracious? Start where Paul starts: with the grace you have received. You do not manufacture grace for others out of your own reserves; you pass on what has been given to you, and you have been given more than you will ever have to give (Ephesians 4:32; Matthew 18:21–35). Feelings often follow obedience rather than leading it. So pray for the person, refuse to rehearse the wrong, speak to them kindly, and take one concrete step toward peace. Grace does not pretend the wrong did not happen, and it does not require you to trust someone who has not changed; but it does let go of the right to pay them back.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s thanksgiving is sincere, and it also lays the ground for the request: Philemon’s known love for all the saints is about to meet a saint he had not counted.
verseByVerse.theology:
An Argument Built from a Man's Own Character

Paul tells Philemon what he already is, and asks him to be it consistently. The words that describe Philemon's reputation in verse 7, hearts and refreshed, come back in verses 12 and 20, applied to Onesimus and to the request.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philemon was known for his love 'for all the saints'.

Now: When you must ask something hard of another Christian, name the grace already at work in them and ask them to extend it to the case they had left out.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers, because I hear of your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank my God always. “You” is singular from here until verse 22: Paul now addresses Philemon personally. The thanksgiving is sincere, and it also lays the ground for the request.

Because I hear. Reports kept coming, perhaps from Epaphras (v. 23) or Onesimus himself. Love is mentioned first, perhaps deliberately, since it is love that Paul will appeal to (v. 9).

Toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints. The sentence crosses: faith is directed to the Lord Jesus; love to all the saints. “All the saints” is the word the whole letter turns on: every believer, including, now, Onesimus. Paul is describing him accurately and then presenting him with a saint he had not counted: until recently, one of his slaves.

The method of the letter. Paul does not begin by telling Philemon what he ought to be. He begins by telling him truthfully what he already is, and then asks him to be it consistently, which is harder to refuse than a rebuke and treats him as an adult rather than a problem.

Faith and love belong together. The saints are not a separate object from the Lord. Paul had learned that on the road to Damascus, when the risen Jesus asked him, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). To harm Christ’s people was to harm Christ, and the reverse is equally true: love for the saints is faith in Christ taking hold of the people he has made his own. So when Onesimus turns up as one more of the saints, Philemon will not be asked to love a new category of person, only to see that the Lord he trusts has already claimed this one.

How do I love all the saints, including Christians I find difficult? By remembering that the word is all, and that the reason you love them is not that they are easy but that Christ loved them. Start with prayer: it is very hard to keep resenting someone you pray for by name. Then act before you feel: greet them, ask how they are, do them a kindness. Look for evidence of grace in them and thank God for it, as Paul did for Philemon. And notice the people in your church whom you have, without meaning to, left out of your all: the new, the awkward, the poor, those from a different background. Onesimus was one of those.

In everyday life. If you need to raise something difficult with someone, begin, honestly and specifically, with what you see of God’s grace in them.

verseByVerse.quote: and I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ. For I have derived much joy and comfort from your love, my brother, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sharing of your faith. Often called the hardest sentence in the letter to translate. “Sharing” is koinōnia: fellowship, partnership, having in common. It means the partnership Philemon has with other believers through their common faith, and the word anticipates v. 17: if you consider me your partner.

May become effective. The word gives us energy: Paul prays that Philemon’s fellowship will actually do something.

Every good thing. The prayer for deep knowledge is not general: the next paragraph presents a specific case. Paul is praying, in advance, for the thing he is about to ask.

Fellowship that begins with the Son. The partnership Paul prays for has its source in a deeper one. God is faithful, he told the Corinthians, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord (1 Corinthians 1:9). Believers share a life with one another because each first shares in Christ: his death, his righteousness, his Spirit, his inheritance. That is every good thing that is in us, and Paul prays that Philemon will know it so deeply that it overflows. A man who sees how much he has been given in Christ finds it far easier to give a runaway what he does not deserve.

The hearts of the saints refreshed. “Hearts” (splanchna) is literally the inward parts, the seat of deep emotion. “Refreshed” means given rest, as for a tired traveller. Watch what Paul does with these two words. In v. 12 he will call Onesimus his own splanchna, my very heart. And in v. 20 he will ask Philemon to refresh his heart in Christ, using the same two words, by refreshing Onesimus. The letter’s argument is being assembled out of the man’s own character.

The King James says the communication of thy faith. Is this about evangelism? Older translations render it that way, and many have read it as a prayer for Philemon’s witness. The word means fellowship or partnership, and the more likely reading is that Paul prays for the generous partnership that flows from Philemon’s faith to bear fruit, which is exactly what he is about to ask of him. Telling others the gospel is commanded elsewhere (Matthew 28:19–20; 1 Peter 3:15), but this verse is about fellowship: the common life believers share, and what it does when it becomes active.

For worship. Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28): the Lord Jesus is the great refresher of weary hearts. He gives rest still, often through the hands of his people: every hot meal set before an exhausted parent, every evening of company for a lonely widow, is his rest passing from one heart to another, a foretaste of the Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here the letter turns from thanks to appeal. Paul names the authority he will not use, introduces the runaway as his own son, and reaches the sentence the letter exists to deliver: a slave is now a brother.
verseByVerse.theology:
Goodness by Compulsion Is Not Goodness

Verse 14 governs the letter: Paul wants Philemon's goodness to be 'of your own accord'. Verse 16 is its heart: a beloved brother, 'both in the flesh and in the Lord'.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A runaway slave met Paul in prison and was sent home as a brother.

Now: There is a real difference between the pressure of authority and the pressure of affection, and only one of them leaves a man free.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required, yet for love's sake I prefer to appeal to you—I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bold enough to command. Here the letter turns, with great restraint. As an apostle, Paul has authority to give orders, and he chooses not to use it. But he names it, so that Philemon knows exactly what is being withheld: not manipulation but its opposite. He puts it on the table and sets it down where it can be seen.

What is required. Receiving Onesimus well is not optional; it is what a Christian ought to do. The outcome is not in doubt; only the manner of reaching it is.

For love’s sake. Either Philemon’s love or the love that binds believers. Command produces compliance; appeal produces something else, and Paul wants the something else. He will say why in v. 14: goodness by compulsion is not goodness.

An old man. Paul was probably in his late fifties or early sixties, worn by beatings, shipwrecks and prison. Some read ambassador (the two Greek words were sometimes spelled alike), but old man fits the tender appeal.

A prisoner also. Paul is trading on his age and his chains. Some have found this uncomfortable, but the pressure of affection, unlike the pressure of authority, leaves a man free. He has spent his life insisting on his apostleship when the gospel was at stake. Here, where only a slave’s future is at stake, he lays it down without a murmur.

Lord and Teacher, with a towel. Paul’s way of naming his authority and then setting it down is not his invention. The night before he died, Jesus took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet, and then said, You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am (John 13:13). He named his authority, and used it to kneel. Paul the apostle, appealing as an old man in chains, is a servant following his Master, and he is asking Philemon to do the same: to use his rights as a master to stoop to a slave.

When should a parent, leader or elder command rather than appeal? Command when the matter is clear, urgent or dangerous, or when appeal has been refused: a child running into the road needs an order, not an invitation, and Paul himself gave firm commands where the gospel or the church’s purity was at stake (2 Thessalonians 3:6; 1 Corinthians 5). But wherever you can, appeal. Explain why, show the person what love and the gospel ask, and let them choose. That is how you grow mature believers rather than compliant ones. Authority that is always used is soon resented; authority that is held in reserve and laid down in love is rarely needed.

For worship. God has every right to command, and he does command; yet over and over he pleads. Come now, let us reason together. Return to me. Be reconciled to God, his ambassadors implore on behalf of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:20). The Lord of glory, who could summon his creatures with a word, stood at the door and knocked. He wins his people not by force but by love, until they come willingly in the day of his power (Psalm 110:3), and the yes he receives from them is the free yes he wanted all along.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment. (Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For my child. In the Greek, the appeal and the relationship come before the name: by the time the name of the man who had run lands, Paul has already claimed him as a son.

Onesimus. The name means useful or profitable, a common slave name, given for the obvious reason.

Whose father I became. Paul led Onesimus to Christ while in chains, and uses the language of spiritual fatherhood (1 Corinthians 4:15; Galatians 4:19). If Paul was in Rome, the runaway had gone to the obvious place to disappear and there met the one man in the empire most likely to send him home. God used Paul’s chains and Onesimus’s flight to save him.

Formerly useless. A wordplay: Useful was useless (achrēston), possibly with a play on Christos as well, since in the pronunciation of the time a-chrēstos may have sounded like without Christ. The wordplay is gentle, and it is an admission. Paul does not pretend the man was a good servant badly treated, and v. 18 allows that he may owe money besides. He concedes the whole charge, and then asks for the man anyway, on entirely different grounds.

But now useful. The word (euchrēston) may have sounded to some ears like good Christ. Conversion has made him what his name said. Grace does not only forgive a man’s past; it makes him worth something (2 Timothy 2:21; 4:11, where the same word is used of Mark).

Useful because he is in Christ. What made the difference? Onesimus had been joined to Christ. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has passed away, behold, the new has come (2 Corinthians 5:17). The Lord who came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45) now lived in a household slave, and the honesty, diligence and faithfulness Paul found in him were Christ’s own life taking shape in a runaway.

How do I know whether someone who wronged me has really changed? Look for the fruit Paul could point to. Onesimus did not merely say he was sorry: he came back to face the man he had wronged, he did not hide the debt, and he had proved himself in service over time. Real repentance owns the wrong without excuses, seeks to put right what can be put right, and shows itself in changed behaviour that lasts (Luke 19:8; 2 Corinthians 7:11). Forgiveness can be given at once; trust is rebuilt over time. You may forgive fully and still wait, wisely, to see the fruit before handing back responsibility.

For worship. We were all once achrēstos, without Christ and of no use to God, and none of us went looking for him. He came after us. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, and he follows runaways down every road they take until he finds them, often in the last place they expected. Then he makes them his children and gives them a name and a usefulness they could never have earned. A slave who ran from his master ran straight into the arms of his Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Onesimus was Philemon’s slave who had run away. His name means “useful,” and Paul plays on it.

verseByVerse.quote: I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart. I would have been glad to keep him with me, in order that he might serve me on your behalf during my imprisonment for the gospel, but I preferred to do nothing without your consent in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am sending him back. Three words in the Greek decide everything, and they come before any of the pleading. Paul does not hide Onesimus, or argue that his conversion has cancelled the legal position. He puts the man on the road to Colossae with a letter in his hand. Under Roman law a returning fugitive could be branded, flogged, or worse, and both men knew it. The appeal is made after the risk has been taken, and Onesimus showed courage and repentance in going.

My very heart. The word of v. 7 (splanchna): Philemon refreshes the hearts of the saints, and Paul is sending him his own. It is what the Father did first: he sent his Son, his very heart, into a hostile world, knowing what it would cost him.

Glad to keep him. Paul wanted him and says so plainly. There is no pretence that returning him was easy or that Onesimus was dispensable.

On your behalf. Paul tactfully suggests that Onesimus’s service would have been Philemon’s gift to Paul, a way to be generous rather than merely deprived, and hints that Philemon might send Onesimus back to serve Paul.

Not by compulsion. Onesimus belonged to Philemon under law, and Paul would not take advantage. This sentence governs the whole letter. Paul could have kept him, or written a letter Philemon could not refuse. He did neither, because good done under compulsion has the shape of goodness and none of the substance (2 Corinthians 9:7). It is also how God deals with people: what he is after is a willing heart. He does not force the will; when he saves, he renews it, giving a new heart that wants what he wants, so that his people obey gladly (Ezekiel 36:26; Philippians 2:13).

Freely, as he gave himself. The principle that goodness must be free is rooted in the cross. Nobody compelled the Son of God: no one took his life from him; he laid it down of himself (John 10:18), and Paul could say of him, he loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). So Paul will not extract a forced kindness from Philemon, because a gospel of free grace cannot be answered with grudging compliance. What he wants from Philemon is what Christ gave Philemon: goodness entirely of its own accord.

Did not the law forbid returning a runaway slave to his master? Deuteronomy 23:15–16 forbade Israel to hand back a slave who had escaped to them from his master. That law protected slaves who fled to Israel from other lands. Paul is sending a brother back to a fellow believer, with a letter that asks him to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul himself (v. 17), so that Onesimus goes back to a changed household, not to punishment. Sadly, slaveholders in later centuries cited this letter to justify returning fugitive slaves; they ignored everything the letter actually asks.

Should a new Christian go back and face the consequences of past wrongs? Often, yes. Conversion cancels guilt before God, but it does not cancel just obligations to people. Zacchaeus repaid what he had taken (Luke 19:8); Onesimus went back. A believer who has stolen should repay where he can; one who has committed a crime may need to confess it to the authorities; one who has wronged a family member should seek them out. Do it wisely, with counsel from your pastor, especially where there are legal implications or where the person wronged might be harmed by contact. The aim is not to earn forgiveness, which Christ has already won, but to walk in the light and put right what can be put right.

verseByVerse.quote: For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever, no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This perhaps is why. Paul does not claim certain knowledge of God’s purposes; he offers Philemon a way of reading his loss. The verb is passive. Paul does not say he ran away, which is what happened, but was parted, hinting at God’s hidden hand. It is Joseph’s delicacy with his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). God’s providence works even through human sin, without excusing it.

Back forever. “For a while” is literally for an hour, set against forever. A few months of loss set against an eternity of brotherhood: Paul is asking Philemon to do the arithmetic. For an hour we may be parted; in Christ we are given back to one another for eternity.

More than a bondservant. Verse 16 carries the letter’s deepest point. Paul does not command manumission. He says something in the long run more corrosive: whatever Onesimus’s legal status, the category has been superseded. Philemon may still hold the legal papers, but he may no longer look at Onesimus and see property. He must see a man for whom Christ died, who will sit beside him at the Lord’s table now and in the life to come.

As a beloved brother. This is the heart of the letter. In Christ, master and slave are brothers, equal members of God’s family (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11). Taken seriously, this would dissolve slavery.

Brothers because of the firstborn. Where does a brotherhood strong enough to outlast slavery come from? From the Son. Christ is the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29), and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). Onesimus and Philemon became brothers the day each became Christ’s, because each was adopted into the same family through the same elder Brother. That is why it is forever: it depends not on Roman law but on Christ, who will never disown either of them. A master who refused to treat Onesimus as a brother would be refusing the very relationship on which his own salvation rested.

In the flesh and in the Lord. In the flesh means in the actual house and the daily arrangements, not merely in a spiritual realm where equality costs nothing. Paul will not let the brotherhood be confined to Sunday.

Where Christians differ: did Paul want Onesimus freed? Some think Paul was silently content for Onesimus to remain a slave; others think he was hinting strongly at freedom. This commentary’s view: Paul does not explicitly demand freedom, but “no longer as a bondservant,” “more than a bondservant,” “receive him as you would receive me” (v. 17), and “you will do even more than I say” (v. 21) all point strongly in that direction. Early tradition suggests an Onesimus later became bishop of Ephesus; if this is the same man, Philemon presumably freed him. More importantly, Paul establishes the principle of brotherhood that makes slavery incompatible with the gospel.

Does the Bible, then, condone slavery? No. Paul’s silence about abolition is not approval. It is honest to admit that the New Testament regulates masters and slaves rather than forbidding slavery outright, and that this troubles many readers. But Paul worked within a society where slavery was everywhere and could not be changed by a letter, but he planted what would destroy it: a slave is a beloved brother, Paul tells slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21, on the most likely reading of a verse some translate differently), and he lists enslavers among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). Roman slavery was also not identical to the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, which began with man-stealing, a crime the law of Moses punished with death (Exodus 21:16). Christian abolitionists in later centuries drew on exactly these truths. The gospel did not overthrow slavery by decree; it set beside it a truth that believers could not consistently hold while owning their brothers, though many Christians took centuries to see it. It is something a slave society could not survive being told: that the man in the kitchen is your brother, in the house as well as in the assembly. Where that was believed, the institution eventually became unthinkable.

How should I read God’s providence in my own losses? With Paul’s perhaps. You may be sure that God works all things for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and you may sometimes see, looking back, what he was doing. But you will not always see it, and you must never use providence to excuse a wrong, your own or someone else’s. Joseph’s brothers were still guilty; Onesimus still owed his master. Hold both: the sin was real, and God was not absent from it. And be slow to explain other people’s suffering to them. Offer a perhaps, gently, only if it comforts.

In everyday life. Pick out one person whose relationship to you is defined mostly by role: the cleaner, the employee, the carer. If they are a believer, they are your brother or sister forever; if not, they bear God’s image. Treat them that way this week, by name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–25 — Receive Him as You Would Receive Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The request itself is one sentence long, and Paul backs it with his own signature on the debt. The letter ends with confidence, a guest room, five names and grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Charge That to My Account

Verses 17-19 enact the gospel rather than explain it: a debt is taken on by another, in writing, and the debtor is to be received 'as you would receive me'.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Welcoming a runaway slave to his table would cost Philemon standing among the slave-owning households of Colossae.

Now: Paul asks for more than private forgiveness and then promises to come and see (v. 22). Reconciliation that must be explained face to face is harder to leave half-done.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you consider me your partner. This is the request, one sentence long. Partner is related to the sharing of v. 6, and the if is not doubt but appeal: since you consider me your partner. Paul is not asking whether Philemon will obey an apostle. He is asking what a partnership is worth when it becomes expensive.

Receive him as me. “Receive” is the word Paul uses of how Christ received us: welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you (Romans 15:7). Not merely forgive him or take him back: receive him with the welcome and standing an apostle and old friend would be given at the door.

What it would cost. A runaway is to be welcomed home as the most honoured guest the house could receive. Philemon’s other slaves will be watching, and neighbours who own slaves will hear; a master who welcomes a runaway to his table would seem to have lost control of his house. Paul is asking Philemon to accept a public humiliation. For a man like Philemon the idol was less likely to be money than standing: being a master whose household obeyed and whose neighbours respected him. The gospel does not flatter that. It asks him to lose face for a brother, as Christ emptied himself and took the form of a servant for us (Philippians 2:7), and the Spirit of that Christ, at work in him, is what makes such a stoop possible.

The deeper pattern. The offender is received on the standing of the one who intercedes, which is precisely how Philemon himself was accepted: Christ presents us to the Father, and the Father receives us as he receives his Son. We are accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6). We came to the Father’s door as runaways, with nothing to offer and a debt behind us, and the Son stood beside us and said, receive him as you would receive me.

Does receiving a repentant person mean ignoring past harm? No. Receiving is welcome, not amnesia. Onesimus’s debt was faced, not denied (v. 18). In a church, a repentant brother is welcomed back to fellowship, to the Lord’s table and to friendship. But where the wrong involved abuse, violence or danger to others, love for the vulnerable still governs: the church must report crimes to the authorities, protect those at risk, and may rightly place limits on where and how the person serves, however sincere his repentance. Forgiveness restores a brother to the family; it does not require placing him where he could harm someone again. Abuse is never to be tolerated or hidden in the name of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it—to say nothing of your owing me even your own self.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If he owes you anything. The if is most likely a courtesy: a runaway could hardly travel far without money, and his absence had cost Philemon his labour. Paul concedes the wrong without dwelling on it, and then does the only thing that actually resolves it.

Charge that to my account. An accounting term: put it on my ledger. Paul is not asking Philemon to absorb the loss; he is offering to pay. Luther wrote that we are all Onesimuses: as Paul took on Onesimus’s debt so that Philemon would receive him, so Christ took on our debt so that the Father would receive us. A man who owes a debt he cannot pay; a third party who assumes it in writing at his own cost; the offended party asked to receive the debtor as though he were the one who paid. Paul has spent his letters arguing that doctrine, and here he simply does it, for a single man.

With my own hand. Whether Paul took the pen from his secretary here or wrote it all, this line is a binding IOU, written into a letter the whole church will hear.

Your own self. The lightest touch in the letter: Paul mentions, while insisting he is not mentioning it, that Philemon, probably converted through him, owes him everything. It is done with a smile, and it is unanswerable. What is a household debt against a man’s own soul?

What does it mean that my debt was charged to Christ? It means that every sin you have committed, against God and against others, was entered on Christ’s account and paid in full at the cross (Isaiah 53:5–6; Colossians 2:13–14). God does not pretend your debt never existed; he transferred it to his Son, who bore its whole penalty. And in exchange, Christ’s perfect obedience is credited to you, so that God receives you as righteous (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 5:19). This is why a believer can have peace with God even on his worst day. The account is not settled by your improvement but by his payment, and it is settled forever.

Does forgiving someone mean cancelling every debt and every consequence? Forgiveness means giving up the right to take revenge and to hold the wrong against the person; it does not always mean every practical debt disappears. Paul does not pretend the money is not owed; he arranges for it to be paid. Sometimes love will cancel a debt outright, as Philemon perhaps did. Sometimes repayment is right and good for the one who did wrong. And where the law has been broken, the courts may still have their say (Romans 13:4). What forgiveness forbids is bitterness, grudge-keeping and personal vengeance.

For worship. The Son of God looked at a debt no sinner could ever pay and took it as his own. He paid in full, with his own blood. The record of debt that stood against us, with its legal demands, he set aside, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14): a sentence written to the very town where Philemon kept his accounts. And we, who owe him our very selves, are not sent a bill. We are received as sons.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably led Philemon to Christ, perhaps during his years at Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Yes, brother, I want some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. At the same time, prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping that through your prayers I will be graciously given to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yes, brother. The very term Paul has asked Philemon to apply to Onesimus (v. 16). “Benefit” (onaimēn) is from the same root as Onesimus, and Paul is punning again: let me have some Onesimus from you.

Refresh my heart. The two words of v. 7: since Onesimus is Paul’s very heart (v. 12), refreshing Onesimus refreshes Paul. He asks for the thing this man is already famous for, in the one case where it will cost him.

Confident of your obedience. Though Paul appealed rather than commanded (vv. 8–9), he still expects obedience. To obey the apostle’s word is to obey Christ.

Even more than I say. What could be more than receiving Onesimus as a brother? The obvious candidate is freedom, and perhaps sending him back to serve Paul in the gospel. Paul leaves the door open without walking through it. He will not name it, because naming it would make it a command and destroy the very thing v. 14 insisted on: goodness freely given.

Prepare a guest room. Paul hopes to be released and to visit: the gentlest possible pressure, said warmly, and also unmistakably an accountability. A decision you will have to explain to someone’s face is a different decision from one you make at a distance.

Through your prayers. The whole church’s prayers, for “your” is plural. Paul believes prayer matters to his release, though the outcome is God’s gift of grace.

In the Lord, in Christ. Twice in one verse Paul names the sphere where all this happens: in the Lord, in Christ. That is why he can be confident. The obedience he expects is not finally to himself. It is obedience to the Lord who had already made Philemon what he was, and who can be trusted to carry the good work he began in him beyond anything Paul dared to ask (Philippians 1:6).

Was Paul released, and did he visit? He expected to be released (compare Philippians 1:25), and the early church believed he was released from his first Roman imprisonment and travelled again before his final arrest; the Pastoral Letters fit that picture (1 Timothy 1:3; Titus 1:5; 2 Timothy 4:13, 20). Whether he reached Colossae, Scripture does not say. What we do know is that he hoped to, and that he expected the prayers of a small house church to be part of how God would answer.

In everyday life. If you have forgiven someone, look for the extra step: the invitation, the gift, the public word of welcome that makes the forgiveness visible.

For worship. God always does more than he says. He promised a seed to Abraham and gave him a multitude; he promised forgiveness and gave adoption, an inheritance, and the Spirit. He is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20). The even more Paul hoped for from Philemon is a small, human echo of the even more that runs through everything God gives.
verseByVerse.note: “Benefit” (onaimēn) plays once more on the name Onesimus, “useful.”

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends greetings to you, and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras, my fellow prisoner. Five names, the same circle as at the close of Colossians (Colossians 4:10–14), one reason the two letters are thought to have travelled together. Epaphras founded the church at Colossae (Colossians 1:7); he was perhaps literally imprisoned with Paul, or voluntarily sharing his confinement.

Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke. Mark, who had turned back from the mission (Acts 13:13; 15:38), now restored (2 Timothy 4:11). Aristarchus, who had suffered with Paul (Acts 27:2). Demas, who is still faithful here, and who would later desert Paul for love of this world (2 Timothy 4:10). Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), who would later be the only one with him (2 Timothy 4:11). The list is sobering: Mark was restored; Demas would fall. Faithfulness today does not guarantee faithfulness tomorrow, except by grace.

Grace be with your spirit. “Your” is plural: everyone in that room. Paul defined this grace elsewhere: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The letter begins (v. 3) and ends with that grace, which is what it has been asking for throughout: that a man made rich by another’s poverty, and received without deserving it, should spend something of himself to receive somebody else the same way. It opened this little letter and it closes it, and it will close the story of every one of his people: received on another’s account, debts paid, brothers forever, home at last.

What happened? We are never told what Philemon did. The letter’s survival is itself good evidence: a document recording a request that had been refused would hardly have been copied and treasured by the church that heard it read. There is a further hint, though it can be put no higher. Some fifty years later Ignatius of Antioch wrote to the church at Ephesus in warm praise of their bishop, a man named Onesimus, and he plays on the name with the very verb of v. 20: may I have joy of you (onaimēn). Whether it is the same man cannot be proved, and the name was common enough. But it is a pleasant thought that the runaway ended his life as a bishop, and that the letter asking for his welcome was kept safe by the churches he served.

Could I fall away like Demas? Demas is a warning that outward service, even at an apostle’s side, does not prove a heart that will endure. Those who finally abandon Christ show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19). But a true believer will be kept: the Lord who began a good work will complete it (Philippians 1:6). The way he keeps us is through warnings like this one, which drive us back to him. So do not presume, and do not despair. If you fear falling, that fear is itself a sign of life; take it to Christ, guard against love for this present world, stay close to his people, and lean on his grace, which held Mark after his failure and can hold you.
verseByVerse.note: The same companions greet the Colossians.

love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints,<sup>6</sup>and I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ.<sup>7</sup>For I have derived much joy and comfort from your love, my brother, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you.<sup>8</sup>Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required,<sup>9</sup>yet for love's sake I prefer to appeal to you—I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner
